newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia mothers prepare for troop release.
newsitem.headline: Colombia mothers prepare for troop release.

text.p: Scores of mothers gathered in this remote jungle town on Saturday to await the release of their sons, soldiers taken prisoner by leftist guerrillas nine months ago.

The inhabitants of this town in southern Caqueta province spruced up the central plaza ready to receive the rebel columns expected to pour in just ahead of Sunday's scheduled handover of the prisoners.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla army, has said it will release the 60 soldiers it seized in a battle in neighbouring Putumayo province last August and also 10 marines captured in a firefight in northwest Choco province in January.
"These months have been very hard for me. I've suffered a lot. Nobody is prepared for this situation," said one of the mothers Maria de Silva Tolosa.

The Aug. 30 raid on the Las Delicias base in Putumayo was one of the FARC's greatest military victories in recent years, political analysts say. It also marked the start of Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis -- largely overshadowed by the recent siege of the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.

Likewise, persuading President Ernesto Samper to temporarily pull the army out of a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) swathe of the province to make way for the release of the prisoners is a major political scoop for the FARC, analysts say.

Cartagena del Chaira is a symbolic choice for the troop handover. It is at the heart of a region famed for the production of coca leaf, the raw material for cocaine production. Some observers suggest the Las Delicias attack was timed to coincide with a wave of peasant protests against the government's forced fumigation of illicit coca crops.
The government accuses the FARC of drug trafficking while the rebels argue poor access and infrastructure across the region leaves peasants with no other form of survival except growing coca.

The FARC has built up a social base in the area. The locals chat with the plainclothes rebels patrolling the streets and refer endearingly to the uniformed guerrillas at strategic checkpoints at the approaches to the town as "los 'chachos", or "the lads".
Even some of the mothers who arrived here last week to prepare for the release of their sons have come to see Colombia's three-decade-old Marxist rebel uprising in a different light.

"This experience has helped me see that the conflict we're suffering is the government's fault. The guerrilla is calling for better conditions for the country...a solution to the problems," said Maria Torres.
Gen. Gabriel Contreras, commander of the army's 12th brigade based in provincial capital Florencia, however, accuses some of the mothers of being "guerrilla spokeswomen" -- charges they reject.

The respected El Espectador newspaper published a poll on Saturday to coincide with the troop release. Of the 600 adults questioned in Colombia's main towns 64 percent said the army was losing the war to the rebels, compared to just 16 percent who said the military were winning.
